newsitem.title: USA: Marvel investors head back to court.
newsitem.headline: Marvel investors head back to court.

text.p: A federal judge in Delaware will decide Thursday whether to lift a restraining order preventing bondholders of Marvel Entertainment Group Inc from voting the 80 percent stake in Marvel's stock that secures their bonds.
If the order is lifted, the bondholders have said they will replace Marvel's board.
That would "bring them a step closer" to implementing the reorganization plan they filed yesterday to lead the company out of bankruptcy, said Alexander Paris, an analyst at Barrington Research.
Marvel, which publishes comic books including Spiderman, The X-Men and The Incredible Hulk, has been operating under bankruptcy protection since December.
But even if the order is lifted, investors and analysts said Marvel would likely ask for another restraining order. Marvel has said it will officially file its own plan soon.
To date, both the Carl Icahn-led bondholders and Ronald Perelman's Andrews Group -- which is Marvel's principal shareholder -- have proposed separate reorganization plans.
The bondholders' plan includes a $365 million rights offering and the creation of a transition team to resuscitate the company led by former Marvel executive Joseph Calamari.

It also gives both Marvel's Fleer/Skybox trading card and Panini sticker businesses, as well as a 10-year secured promissory note, to bank lenders, who seek repayment of their roughly $700 million in loans to the company.

Marvel's plan, on the other hand, looks to spinoff the company's comic book-publishing and licensing operations and merge them with Toy Biz Inc Inc, which is about 27 percent-owned by Marvel. Fleer/Skybox and Panini would then be sold, and bondholders would get warrants to buy up to 12.5 percent in the Marvel-Toy Biz company.

Both sides have blasted each others' plans. Bondholders have also said that since the company did not file its plan by Monday it missed its deadline to do so, and now is not permitted to file a plan under bankruptcy law.
Marvel denied the assertion, saying any party was free to propose a reorganization plan.

Analysts, who claim Marvel is flush with intangible value in its character assets, said the warring is only hurting the company. The market remains skeptical that the sides will soon agree on any reorganization plan, they added.
Marvel's shares closed Wednesday at 2-1/8, down 1/8, while Toy Biz shares closed down 1/4 at 9-3/4.
"The lawyers are probably the only ones making money on all this," according to Paris, who said his firm's clients are no longer interested in holding Marvel shares.
Other analysts said they do not expect the warring to end anytime soon.
Said Smith Barney analyst Jill Krutick of tomorrow's hearing, "There's going to be a lot of hot tempers in that courtroom."
